1.3.1:
Why this matters

The charter is the contract between the project team and the business. It says what problem will be solved, why it matters, what success looks like, and what is in and out of bounds. A weak charter is the most common root cause of failed projects: unclear goals, endless scope, no support. On the exam, charter questions usually ask you to spot a badly written problem or goal statement.

The big idea

Before any data is collected, the team and the sponsor agree in writing on the answers to six questions:

  1. Why does this matter to the business? (business case)
  2. What exactly is wrong? (problem statement)
  3. What will we achieve, by when? (goal statement)
  4. What are we working on, and not working on? (scope)
  5. Who is involved? (team and roles)
  6. When will it be done, and with what? (timeline, resources)

The sponsor signs the charter. From then on, it is the reference point for every tollgate review.

Elements of a charter

Business case. Why this project, why now, in business terms: cost, revenue, customer, strategy, compliance. "Damage claims cost $480,000 last year and our largest customer has said claims are the main reason it is reviewing our contract."

Problem statement. A factual description of the problem: what is wrong, where, when (since when, how often), and how big (the extent, with numbers). It contains no cause, no solution and no blame.

Goal statement. What the project will achieve, written SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. It usually states the baseline, the target and the deadline: "Reduce damage claims from 3.1 to 1.5 per 1,000 loads by December 31."

Scope. The process boundaries (start and stop points, see 1.2.1) and what is explicitly in scope and out of scope: which sites, products, customers, steps.

Team and roles. Sponsor, champion, process owner, belt leading the project, team members, and how much time each gives.

Timeline and milestones. Target dates for each DMAIC tollgate.

Resources, constraints and assumptions. Budget, data access, people, and limits such as "no capital spending" or "no changes to the union agreement".

Risks. What might stop the project, and how the team will handle it.

Sign-off. Signatures of the sponsor and key stakeholders.

Writing a good problem statement

Use this checklist: what, where, when, how big, and what impact.

Bad: "Drivers are careless and we need a new load-securing system."

  • Blames people ("careless").
  • Jumps to a solution ("new system").
  • No numbers, no time frame, no location.

Good: "Since January, damage claims at the Dallas and Memphis terminals have averaged 3.1 per 1,000 loads, versus 1.2 at other terminals, costing $40,000 a month in claims."

  • What: damage claims. Where: Dallas and Memphis. When: since January. How big: 3.1 per 1,000, $40,000 a month. No cause, no solution, no blame.

A problem statement that names the cause or the fix assumes the answer. If the team is wrong about the cause, the whole project is pointed the wrong way.

Scope and "boiling the ocean"

A project that tries to fix too much ("improve all customer service across the company") will not finish. A Green Belt project should normally be completable in about 3 to 6 months by a small team. If the scope is too large, break it into several projects.

Scope creep is when the project quietly grows: new sites, new problems, new requests. The charter is the defense: anything outside the agreed scope needs the sponsor's approval to add.

Stakeholders and communication

  • Stakeholder analysis lists everyone affected by or able to affect the project and rates their current and needed support (for example, from "strongly against" to "strongly supportive"), so the team knows whom to win over.
  • RACI chart: for each task, who is Responsible (does it), Accountable (owns the outcome, only one person), Consulted (gives input before) and Informed (told after).
  • Communication plan: who gets what information, how, and how often.

Choosing the right projects

Organizations have more possible projects than people to run them. Common selection tools:

  • Strategic alignment: does it support the organization's goals?
  • Impact/effort matrix (also called a PICK chart): plot each idea by benefit and difficulty. High benefit, low effort first; low benefit, high effort never.
  • Benefit vs resources: expected savings or customer impact compared with the people, time and money needed.
  • Data availability: Six Sigma needs data. A project with no way to measure the Y is a poor candidate.
  • Known solution? If the fix is already known and just needs doing, it is a "just do it" task, not a DMAIC project.

Worked example

Evaluate this draft goal: "Improve on-time delivery significantly."

  • Specific? No: improve how?
  • Measurable? No: no number.
  • Time-bound? No: no date.

Rewrite: "Increase on-time delivery for the Southeast region from 88% to 95% by June 30." It now has a scope (Southeast), a baseline (88%), a target (95%) and a deadline (June 30).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • A problem statement with a solution in it is wrong. "We need new software" belongs nowhere in a problem statement.
  • A problem statement with a cause in it is wrong. "Late deliveries caused by new drivers" assumes what Analyze should prove.
  • A goal without a baseline or deadline is not SMART.
  • The sponsor signs the charter, not the belt alone.
  • Too-big scope is a selection mistake, not a sign of ambition.

Check yourself

  1. Name four elements of a project charter.
  2. What four things should a problem statement state, and what three things should it never contain?
  3. Rewrite as SMART: "Reduce invoice errors."
  4. In a RACI chart, how many people can be Accountable for a task?
  5. A sponsor asks you to "also look at the Atlanta terminal" halfway through. What is this, and what should happen?
Show answers
  1. Any four of: business case, problem statement, goal statement, scope, team and roles, timeline, resources, constraints and assumptions, risks, sign-off.
  2. What, where, when and how big (extent). Never a cause, a solution or blame.
  3. For example: "Reduce invoice errors from 4.2% to under 1% of invoices by September 30."
  4. One.
  5. Scope creep. It should be evaluated and formally added to the charter (with timeline and resources adjusted), or handled as a separate project.

Key takeaways

  • The charter is the signed agreement: business case, problem, goal, scope, team, timeline, resources, risks.
  • Problem statement: what, where, when, how big; no cause, solution or blame.
  • Goal statement: SMART, with baseline, target and deadline.
  • Control scope; break oversized projects up.
  • Choose projects by strategic fit, impact versus effort, and data availability.
1.3.2:
Why this matters

A project is judged by its metrics. Pick the wrong one and you can "succeed" while the business gets worse: faster deliveries with more damage, lower costs with angrier customers. Good metrics define success honestly and catch side effects.

The big idea

Every project has three kinds of metrics:

  1. Primary metric: the main measure of success. It is the project's Y, tied directly to the problem statement. There should be one.
  2. Secondary metrics: other measures that help explain or support the primary, such as the components of the Y.
  3. Consequential (balancing) metrics: measures that could get worse because of the project. They guard against sub-optimization: improving one thing by hurting another.

Example, a project to cut loading time:

  • Primary: average minutes to load a trailer.
  • Secondary: minutes waiting for a door, minutes waiting for freight.
  • Balancing: damage claims per 1,000 loads, injuries. If loading gets faster but damage rises, the project has not truly succeeded.

Defining a metric properly

Each metric needs:

  • An operational definition (exactly what is measured and how, see 1.2.2).
  • A baseline: current performance, measured in the Measure phase.
  • A target: the goal from the charter.
  • A data type:
  • Continuous (variable) data can take any value on a scale: time, weight, cost, temperature. It carries more information, so smaller samples are needed.
  • Discrete (attribute) data comes in categories or counts: pass/fail, number of defects, on time or late. It is easier to collect but needs larger samples.

Choosing continuous data when possible makes analysis much more powerful. "Minutes late" tells you more than "late yes/no".

Process vs outcome, leading vs lagging

  • Outcome metrics measure the result the customer sees: on-time delivery rate, claims, satisfaction.
  • Process metrics measure how the work is done: dock door wait time, percent of loads with complete paperwork at departure.
  • Lagging indicators report what already happened: last month's claims. Reliable, but too late to prevent anything.
  • Leading indicators predict future results: percent of trailers inspected for securing before departure. They let you act before the outcome suffers.

Good projects watch the outcome (the Y) and manage the process and leading indicators (the X's). That is "monitor the Y, control the X's" from 1.1.4.

Typical Six Sigma metrics

  • Quality: DPMO, defect rate, first time yield, rolled throughput yield (1.2.5).
  • Capability: Cp, Cpk, sigma level (2.4, 1.1.1).
  • Speed: cycle time, lead time, on-time rate.
  • Cost: cost of poor quality (1.2.3), cost per unit.
  • Customer: satisfaction scores, complaints, net promoter score.

Worked example

A project charter says: "Reduce time to issue customer credits from 9 days to 3 days." Suggest metrics.

  • Primary: days from credit approval to credit issued (continuous).
  • Secondary: days waiting for manager approval; days in accounting queue.
  • Balancing: percentage of credits issued in error (speed must not cause wrong credits); customer complaints about credits.
  • Leading indicator: number of credits waiting more than 2 days in any queue.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • No balancing metric. A project that speeds up a process can damage quality. The balancing metric catches it.
  • Several primary metrics. One primary metric keeps the project focused.
  • Discrete when continuous is available. "Late or not" throws away how late.
  • Only lagging indicators. You see problems only after they have hurt customers.

Check yourself

  1. What is the purpose of a consequential (balancing) metric?
  2. Is "number of late loads" continuous or discrete? What continuous alternative is there?
  3. Classify: "monthly customer complaints" as leading or lagging.
  4. A project's primary metric is hold time in a call center. Name a balancing metric.
  5. Why prefer continuous data?
Show answers
  1. To detect if improving the primary metric makes something else worse (sub-optimization).
  2. Discrete (a count). Continuous alternative: minutes late for each load.
  3. Lagging.
  4. For example, first-call resolution rate or customer satisfaction, because rushing calls could hurt them.
  5. It contains more information, so it needs smaller samples and supports more powerful analysis.

Key takeaways

  • Primary (the Y), secondary (supporting), consequential/balancing (side effects).
  • Each metric needs an operational definition, baseline, target and data type.
  • Continuous data is more informative than discrete.
  • Outcome vs process metrics; lagging vs leading indicators.
1.3.3:
Why this matters

Companies fund projects that pay off. Being able to estimate and classify a project's financial benefit is how you win approval and prove success. The exam asks you to classify benefits and compute ROI and payback, and sometimes to choose which project to fund.

The big idea

Benefits come in two kinds, and the difference is whether money actually moves:

  • Hard savings: real cash that shows up on the profit and loss statement (P&L). Budgets can be reduced, or revenue goes up.
  • Soft savings: real value that does not directly change the P&L: freed capacity, avoided future costs, time saved, better satisfaction.

Hard vs soft, with examples

BenefitHard or softWhy
Overtime cut by $60k a yearHardPayroll spending actually falls
Damage claims cut by $120k a yearHardCash paid out falls
Fuel cost reduced by $0.04 a mileHardFuel bills fall
Dispatchers save 10 hours a week, but no one is let go or reassignedSoftCapacity freed, but costs unchanged
Avoided buying a second forklift next yearSoft (cost avoidance)Money never spent, but no budget line falls
Customer satisfaction up 8 pointsSoftValuable, but not cash

Soft savings can become hard when the freed capacity is actually used: the saved dispatcher hours absorb growth so no new hire is needed, or a contractor is released.

Ways projects create value

  • Cost reduction: spend less on something you already spend on (hard).
  • Revenue growth: sell more, keep customers, charge for better service (hard if it can be traced).
  • Cost avoidance: prevent a future cost that would otherwise occur (usually soft).

Return on investment (ROI)

ROI compares net benefit with cost:

ROI = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost

A project costs $25,000 (training, equipment, team time) and saves $100,000 in its first year. ROI = (100,000 − 25,000) ÷ 25,000 = 3.0, or 300%.

Payback period

Payback is how long it takes for the benefits to repay the investment. When the yearly benefit is constant:

Payback period = investment ÷ annual benefit

A $40,000 dock leveler that saves $16,000 a year pays back in 40,000 ÷ 16,000 = 2.5 years.

When benefits are uneven, add them year by year until the total reaches the investment. Investment $50,000; savings of $10,000, $20,000, $30,000 in years 1 to 3. Cumulative: $10k, $30k, $60k. Payback happens during year 3: after year 2, $20,000 is still needed out of year 3's $30,000, so payback is 2 + 20/30 ≈ 2.67 years.

NPV and IRR (awareness only)

A dollar next year is worth less than a dollar today. Net present value (NPV) discounts future benefits back to today's value and subtracts the cost. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the company's required return. Internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate at which NPV equals zero. Green Belts mostly need to know what these are; finance usually calculates them.

Capturing the benefits

  • Finance validation: many companies require the finance department to agree on the baseline and verify savings before they are claimed.
  • Tracking: benefits are typically tracked for about 12 months after the project closes, to confirm they last. This is common company practice, not an IASSC rule.
  • Ownership: the process owner keeps the gains; the control plan protects them.

Worked example: which project to fund?

Project AProject B
Cost$20,000$60,000
Annual hard savings$30,000$45,000
Payback0.67 years1.33 years
First-year ROI0.5 (50%)−0.25 (−25%)

If money is tight and the goal is a quick return, A wins: faster payback, positive first-year ROI. B saves more per year, so over a long horizon B produces more total savings; a judgment call might still fund B if it supports a strategic goal. Questions at the "Evaluate" level expect you to weigh payback, ROI, strategic fit and risk together.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling freed capacity hard savings. It is soft unless costs actually fall.
  • Cost avoidance is soft. Nothing in the current budget goes down.
  • ROI uses net benefit (benefit minus cost) on top. Benefit ÷ cost alone is a benefit-cost ratio, not ROI.
  • Payback with uneven cash flows needs a cumulative total, not a single division.

Check yourself

  1. Is "avoided hiring a planned second shift supervisor" hard or soft?
  2. A project costs $15,000 and saves $45,000. What is ROI?
  3. A $90,000 system saves $30,000 a year. What is payback?
  4. Investment $30,000; savings $5,000, $15,000, $20,000 in years 1 to 3. When does it pay back?
  5. Why might finance need to validate savings?
Show answers
  1. Soft (cost avoidance): no current budget line falls.
  2. (45,000 − 15,000) ÷ 15,000 = 2.0, or 200%.
  3. 90,000 ÷ 30,000 = 3 years.
  4. Cumulative: 5k, 20k, 40k. After year 2, 10k is still needed out of year 3's 20k, so 2.5 years.
  5. To make sure the baseline and claimed savings are real and agreed, so the numbers are credible.

Key takeaways

  • Hard savings change the P&L; soft savings (capacity, cost avoidance, satisfaction) do not directly.
  • ROI = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost.
  • Payback = investment ÷ annual benefit when constant; use cumulative totals when uneven.
  • NPV and IRR account for the time value of money; awareness level.
  • Finance validates savings; benefits are commonly tracked for about a year.
